items.title: Conditions
items.body: Fixed number of trials \(n\); each trial has two outcomes (success/failure); constant probability \(p\); trials independent. Then \(X\sim B(n,p)\).

items.title: Cumulative Probabilities
items.body: Use tables or calculator: \(P(X\leq r)\). Note: \(P(X\geq r)=1-P(X\leq r-1)\).

items.title: Normal Approximation
items.body: If \(n\) large and \(p\) close to 0.5: \(X\approx N(np,\,np(1-p))\) with continuity correction.

items.title: Finding Unknown n or p
items.body: Set up equations using given probabilities and solve. May require trial and error or logarithms for \(n\).

body.en: If \(X\sim B(n,p)\): \(n\) independent trials, each with probability \(p\) of success. \(P(X=r)=\dbinom{n}{r}p^r(1-p)^{n-r}\). Mean: \(E(X)=np\). Variance: \(\text{Var}(X)=np(1-p)\). Use the binomial distribution when: fixed \(n\), trials independent, constant \(p\), only 2 outcomes (success/failure).

Probabilistic Normalization & Moment Structure: Every probability model is governed by total probability conservation: \(\sum_x P(X=x) = 1\) for discrete random variables and \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1\) (with \(f(x) \ge 0\)) for continuous density functions. Expected value \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) acts as a linear operator (\(\mathbb{E}[aX + bY] = a\mathbb{E}[X] + b\mathbb{E}[Y]\)), whereas variance scales quadratically and adds for independent variables: \(\operatorname{Var}(aX \pm bY) = a^2\operatorname{Var}(X) + b^2\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).

body.en:
Inequality bounds for discrete distributions: Unlike continuous variables, strict inequalities make a critical difference:
• \(P(X \ge r) = 1 - P(X \le r - 1)\) (NOT \(1 - P(X \le r)\))
• \(P(X > r) = 1 - P(X \le r)\)
• \(P(X < r) = P(X \le r - 1)\).

'At least one' complement shortcut: \(P(X \ge 1) = 1 - P(X = 0) = 1 - (1-p)^n\). Always look for this time-saving identity in exam questions.

Four binomial conditions: Cambridge exam questions frequently ask you to state assumptions justifying the binomial model: (1) Fixed number of trials \(n\), (2) Constant probability of success \(p\), (3) Independent trials, (4) Exactly two mutually exclusive outcomes (success/failure).

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Binomial Distribution)

body.en:
Why Variance Scales as \(a^2\) and Independent Variances Always Add: By definition, \(\operatorname{Var}(Y) = \mathbb{E}[(Y - \mu_Y)^2]\). For \(Y = aX - bW\) with independent \(X, W\), subtracting its mean \(\mu_Y = a\mu_X - b\mu_W\) gives:

\[ \operatorname{Var}(aX - bW) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[(a(X - \mu_X) - b(W - \mu_W))^2\right] = a^2\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu_X)^2] - 2ab\,\operatorname{Cov}(X,W) + b^2\mathbb{E}[(W-\mu_W)^2] \]

Because independence implies \(\operatorname{Cov}(X, W) = 0\), the cross term vanishes and \((-b)^2 = +b^2\), proving \(\operatorname{Var}(aX - bW) = a^2\operatorname{Var}(X) + b^2\operatorname{Var}(W)\). Uncertainty compounds whether random variables are added or subtracted.

The mean of \(X\sim B(n,0.4)\) is 6. Find \(n\) and the standard deviation.

\[np=6\Rightarrow n=15.\quad\sigma=\sqrt{15\times0.4\times0.6}=\sqrt{3.6}\approx1.90.\]

Problem (Medium): A factory produces light bulbs. The probability that a randomly selected light bulb is defective is \(p\). The number of defective light bulbs in a random sample of \(n\) bulbs follows a binomial distribution \(X \sim B(n, p)\). It is known that the mean number of defective bulbs in a sample of \(n=25\) is \(2\). \\ (i) Calculate the value of \(p\). \\ (ii) For a sample of \(n=50\) bulbs, calculate the probability of finding exactly \(k\) defective bulbs, where \(k\) is the smallest integer such that \(P(X \le k) > 0.9\). \\ (iii) If a sample of \(n=50\) bulbs is taken, find the smallest value of \(n'\) such that the probability of observing at least one defective bulb is greater than \(0.999\).

Step-by-Step Solution: Part (i): For a binomial distribution \(X \sim B(n, p)\), the mean is given by \(E(X) = np\). \\ We are given \(n=25\) and \(E(X)=2\). \\ So, \(25p = 2\), which gives \(p = \frac{2}{25} = 0.08\). \\ Part (ii): Now, \(n=50\) and \(p=0.08\). The number of defective bulbs follows \(X \sim B(50, 0.08)\). \\ We need to find the smallest integer \(k\) such that \(P(X \le k) > 0.9\). \\ We can use a binomial cumulative distribution table or a calculator. \\ Let's calculate a few values: \(P(X \le 3) = P(X=0) + P(X=1) + P(X=2) + P(X=3)\) Using a binomial CDF calculator or table for \(B(50, 0.08)\): \\ \(P(X \le 3) \approx 0.4503 \) \(P(X \le 4) \approx 0.6333 \) \(P(X \le 5) \approx 0.7918 \) \(P(X \le 6) \approx 0.8941 \) \(P(X \le 7) \approx 0.9575 \) The smallest integer \(k\) for which \(P(X \le k) > 0.9\) is \(k=7\). \\ Part (iii): We have \(n=50\) and \(p=0.08\). We want to find the smallest value of \(n'\) such that the probability of observing at least one defective bulb is greater than \(0.999\). \\ The probability of observing at least one defective bulb is \(P(X \ge 1) = 1 - P(X=0)\). \\ For a binomial distribution, \(P(X=0) = \binom{n'}{0} p^0 (1-p)^{n'} = (1-p)^{n'}\). \\ So we need \(1 - (1-p)^{n'} > 0.999\). \\ Substituting \(p=0.08\), we get \(1 - (0.92)^{n'} > 0.999\). \\ This means \((0.92)^{n'} < 1 - 0.999 = 0.001\). \\ Taking the natural logarithm of both sides: \(n' \ln(0.92) < \ln(0.001)\). \\ Since \(\ln(0.92)\) is negative, we must reverse the inequality sign when dividing: \(n' > \frac{\ln(0.001)}{\ln(0.92)}\). \\ \(n' > \frac{-6.907755...}{-0.083381...}\) \(n' > 82.847...\) The smallest integer value of \(n'\) is \(83\). \\ The question asks for the smallest value of \(n'\) for a sample of size \(n=50\). This part of the question seems to imply a re-sampling or a different scenario for \(n'\). Assuming \(n'\) refers to the sample size for a new calculation of the probability of at least one defective bulb.

Problem (Hard): A fair coin is tossed 3 times. Let X be the number of heads obtained. What is the probability that X = 2?

Step-by-Step Solution: This is a binomial distribution scenario. The number of trials is \(n=3\) (the number of coin tosses). The probability of success (getting a head) in a single trial is \(p = \frac{1}{2}\), and the probability of failure (getting a tail) is \(q = 1-p = \frac{1}{2}\). We want to find the probability of getting exactly \(k=2\) heads. The binomial probability formula is \(P(X=k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k q^{n-k}\). Substituting the values: \(P(X=2) = \binom{3}{2} (\frac{1}{2})^2 (\frac{1}{2})^{3-2}\) \(P(X=2) = \binom{3}{2} (\frac{1}{2})^2 (\frac{1}{2})^1\) First, calculate the binomial coefficient \(\binom{3}{2}\). This represents the number of ways to choose 2 heads from 3 tosses: \(\binom{3}{2} = \frac{3!}{2!(3-2)!} = \frac{3!}{2!1!} = \frac{3 \times 2 \times 1}{(2 \times 1) \times 1} = 3\). Now, substitute this back into the probability formula: \(P(X=2) = 3 \times (\frac{1}{4}) \times (\frac{1}{2})\) \(P(X=2) = 3 \times \frac{1}{8}\) \(P(X=2) = \frac{3}{8}\). Alternatively, we can list all possible outcomes for 3 coin tosses (H for heads, T for tails): HHH, HHT, HTH, THH, HTT, THT, TTH, TTT. There are \(2^3 = 8\) total possible outcomes. The outcomes with exactly 2 heads are: HHT, HTH, THH. There are 3 such outcomes. Therefore, the probability of getting exactly 2 heads is \(\frac{\text{Number of favorable outcomes}}{\text{Total number of outcomes}} = \frac{3}{8}\).

rows.en: Produces smaller or even negative variance for the difference of independent variables.
Always add variances of independent variables: \(\sigma_{X-Y}^2 = \sigma_X^2 + \sigma_Y^2\).
Confuses the variance of the sample mean \(\sigma^2/n\) with its standard error.
Absence of sufficient evidence against \(H_0\) does not prove \(H_0\) is true.
Write in context: "There is insufficient evidence at the \(\alpha\) level to reject \(H_0\)."

body.en: Exam Marking Tip (Cambridge International AS Level (9709 Paper 1 / Paper 4 / Paper 5)): Always state the distribution parameters explicitly (e.g., \(X \sim \operatorname{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) or \(\bar{X} \sim \operatorname{N}(\mu, \sigma^2/n)\)) and sketch a quick shaded bell curve before standardizing to \(z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\). This secures the method mark even if a rounding slip occurs later.
